posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
Because I'll need to have my fancy new (yes I'm happy with it ) 315 close to the table I'd rather not use a fan to cool the heat sink. I'm likely to use it for extended periods of time and want to make sure it stays coolish.

It's got a large heat sink now with deep fins and I've thought about putting it in a tub partly filled with mineral oil. Various people have used mineral oil to liquid cool PCs as well as to totally submerge them for [full-motherboard](http://www.russellware.com/liquidlinux/) cooling insanity.

Can anyone think of serious downsides to the idea of submerging this heat sink

![Image](http://www.dragonseye.com/gallery/d/5550-4/GreenLaser.jpg)

halfway in mineral oil?

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md: Sounds like an uneccesary, messy proposition. The heat will go into the mineral oil - then where? Why not put the heat sink in a box, and duct some fan-driven air thru it using dryer vent hose? You can then direct the intake and exit air anywhere you like (such as into the next room). With that huge heat sink, you wouldn't have to move much air to keep the temp down.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **Tony:** Sounds like an uneccesary, messy proposition. The heat will go into the mineral oil - then where?

I don't expect the laser to generate all that much heat. It's been fairly cold in my office today and I've been running the laser for about five hours at 100mW and it's just barely warm to the touch.

There would be about a gallon of mineral oil which forms a fairly large thermal mass. The whole mass would heat up much more slowly than the heat sink alone and I probably wouldn't need a fan, even in the summer.

> **Tony:** Why not put the heat sink in a box, and duct some fan-driven air thru it using dryer vent hose?

I'm vibration-phobic Being on a 2nd floor that's wood, I've got to fight vibrations more than many others on the forum. The laser will actually be on a frame that's touching the table.

Also that's much more work than plunking the heat sink into some liquid.

> **Tony:** With that huge heat sink, you wouldn't have to move much air to keep the temp down.

True.

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md: The fan can be at the other end of the hose, well removed from the table. Gentle, laminar flow thru the hose wouldn't add significant vibration, IMHO. Also, the laser mount doesn't *have to* touch the table - it can be isolated from it.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **Tony:** The fan can be at the other end of the hose, well removed from the table. Gentle, laminar flow thru the hose wouldn't add significant vibration, IMHO.

Probably not. If I go that route I could always wire the fans into my controller and turn them off during settling and back on afterwards.

> **Tony:** Also, the laser mount doesn't *have to* touch the table - it can be isolated from it.

Unless I'm floating it on a magical cushion of Magicalness(tm) it'll never be fully isolated and I can't put it on a separate table as my floor flexes too much.

I guess the biggest advantage liquid has for me is that I can make it work with a minimum of fuss. Wiring, cabling, fans and conduits are fussy.

posts.author: Gary Deal
posts.content_md:
There's another option for using the cooling capacity of the heatsink that wouldn't be vibration-heavy. Basically, put the finned section in a box, with a "flue" on one side and leave the other side open. The warm air will find it's way into the flue and rise, sucking air through the fins. Any idea how much air you'll need to flow to maintain a desired temp? (I don't have any idea) It should be easy enough to test with some cardboard, tape, and a paper towel core. I've been told that the longer the flue/taller the chimney, the more draw you'll get into the fireplace.

If airflow in the optical area would be a problem, a couple more towel cores would provide external ductwork to outside the curtain. A final design could use flexible clothes-dryer ducting (cheap).

An alternate idea, anyway, the oil sounds scary.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I think the most important thing here is to accurately measure the temperature of the laser head for an extended period.

A couple of recommendations, Michael: if you don't have it already, I would suggest getting a copy of the 315M operator's manual. On page 2-5, is says that the maximum temperature for the laser head baseplate is 130F for the 315M-100, and 113F for the 315M-150. This is the stated maximum, probably you will want to keep it cooler than this.

Also, if you don't have one already, I would suggest getting an infrared non-contact thermometer to obtain accurate measurements. These have become very cheap recently. I think they are available for about $20 or less from Harbor Freight. These thermometers are very, very useful.

The heat sink in the photo already looks pretty good. If you need something better, I would suggest using 1/2 aluminum plate of whatever dimensions are necessary. Whatever you use, just monitor the temperature of the baseplate (not the heatsink, but the baseplate of the laser head itself -- the parts that stick out about 3/8 inch on the bottom of the front and rear). "If it works, it works."
